That sounds awful. I'll tell you why: the core of the game is about the goal, and the obstacles in the way of the goal. Therefore, the players must be given the tools to overcome the challenges. Civilization has a branching tech tree, so if your enemies are focusing on one part of the tech tree, you can tech in another part and exploit a weakness there. In Mario, you are given controls on how to play, including a jump feature. Obfuscating core parts of the player's abilities is the completely wrong way to make a game "mysterious" and "random". A player who does not know what direction to go to achieve the goal will never be able to achieve it, and soon abandon the game because it's not going anywhere.

This also breaks another idea of good game design: good game design pushes the player towards achieving the goal. Your design encourages players to make bad choices. "I'm going to use this dagger because it casts a fireball on occasion," ignoring that that weapon dropped then they were at level 10 (obfuscated, of course), and a much better weapon that doesn't cast fireballs is ignored because it doesn't look cool. The player who then does what he likes is wrongly punished because the game doesn't give him enough information on if he's doing the right thing.

Min/Maxers are gonna min/max. The solution shouldn't be to make min/maxing impossible, but to make sure even off-beat builds are capable, or to make it clear the path is doable, but difficult. If a build is completely bonkers and is the "correct" choice, it is not the fault of the players. It is due to bad game design. Game designers should be testing the game and figuring these things out.

the core of the game is about the goal

Simply incorrect and permanently dismissed after immediately thinking about Minecraft.

All Minecraft players have a goal. The goal doesn't have to be set by the game, but all players of a game always have a goal in mind. Otherwise, they simply wouldn't play. Minecraft players want to build something, that's the goal. No Minecraft players just want to click on the ground, doing nothing. Games are always about the goal. Always. No exceptions. Otherwise, it is not a game. Introduce anyone to Crusader Kings, tell them about everything you can do in the game. The question that is almost always first is: "How do you win?"

I'm going to have to disagree with that premise. It's all about extent of damage doing the wrong thing, and balancing things in a way that encourages experimentation.

Take Tomb Raider. Navigating the jumps correctly is the right thing. Navigating them badly is the wrong thing, sure, but falling to your instant death with a save point a couple of seconds away is less annoying than falling to a lower path that you have to retread for 10 minutes to get back and try again. The goal is clear: get across this area.

The goal for a dungeon crawl kind of game with obfuscated gear is still clear. Kill the baddies, get deeper/escape higher, continue. Eventually the weapon that occasionally casts fireballs will stop being so effective and that drop in effectiveness will encourage the player to give some other drops or treasures a try. There could be clear signals that it's less effective, like visible magical shields that for some reason are keeping the fireball explosions from happening in a monster's face, or it could be subtle, like the corpse not having burn marks. This cycle would happen slowly but still frequently enough that the player can learn that they can't just keep using the same stuff all the time, just like in a fighting game learning that spamming a single attack won't work forever. Either way, the punishment shouldn't be sudden full-out immunity, but eased into, it wouldn't be frustrating.

It would be really helpful if the description gave hints that the player would eventually learn and recognize. Weapons that make my limbs feel numb might be better against animals, armor that feels lighter than it looks might increase my speed. BUT it would be important to be varied and subtle in those descriptions to prevent the player from just doing the translation in their head: swords of ogre decapitation are always blue, boots of improved sneaking are always black, and so on.

Where I agree that it could be awful is because then it becomes a question of whether gear is random and obscured or just obscured. Oh, you found a rusty sword that actually is a magical sword of massacre that will turn everything it touches into hamburger in the first room? Well, I found a polished sword that actually is a balsa wood movie prop. That's going to be pretty boring for both players. Non-random items will get spoiled in FAQs in practically no time at all.

I'm sure there's a middle ground that can be reached, and I would definitely play a game.

You can encourage experimentation without obfuscating core parts of how the game functions. All computer games are based on a little bit of math, simply due to running on computers. In fact, almost all games with some competitive or random aspect have some element of math in them, simply due to the need to balance the strengths and weaknesses of play styles. It doesn't hurt experimentation at all if some of the math is out in the open. The key parts of making the game feel fun and not require min-maxing is to have strengths and weaknesses not related to the raw damage or performance of the ability in question. Say, two competing abilities and while there are damage differences between them, they have properties such as melee or ranged, slow or fast, single target or sweeping, that set the abilities apart. It's no longer about min-maxing, but about matching the type of damage to your playstyle.

Say, you like using powerful single-target melee abilities because you are able to carefully separate enemies and pick them off one-by-one; or you like running straight into a horde, sweeping the lot of them, and emerging unscathed. You can't min-max those differences, because those differences are inherently not based on math. But, the damage they do is all there for the players to see, so they know whether the damage they're doing is effective, and whether new gear upgrades are really upgrades. Obfuscation of core game math isn't needed to have a game that's flavorful and fun.
